ranking.reason: This is the name every panel member would remember and pass on. The proverb «جارك القريب ولا خيّك البعيد» carries the trust and nearby promise for free, and phrases like «اسأل جارك» or «نزّلها على جارك» sound natural from Qamishli to Deir ez-Zor. In Arabic script the word reads for both genders. The only real flaw is the German 'Yarak' echo, and that mostly affects diaspora, not users inside Syria.

It is the most naturally Syrian and modern-playful word on the list. Every age group says it many times a day, and it suggests a fair deal («زبطت البيعة») without overpromising. It ranks below Jarak because it says nothing about 'nearby', and because it is such a common filler word that it sometimes won't be heard as a brand in conversation.

It is clean and easy to say in every region, with no ق/ع trouble, and it sounds like 'a win'. But it feels promotional and Egyptian/MSA (Syrians say لقطة), and for a Homs mother selling furniture out of need, 'profit' feels a little cold. Users will also find other apps with the same name in the store.

It is the exact verb every Syrian already uses for posting an ad, so it is pan-Syrian and punchy. As a name, though, it sounds clumsy in speech («نزّلتها على نزّل»), it reads as 'download' in the stores, and teenagers will joke about it. It works better as the post button than as the brand.

It is very memorable and fun for western Syrians: it is the first comment under every Facebook sale post, so the Aleppo student and the Damascus shopkeeper would grin at it. But the east says بيش/شكد, the ق/أ split shows region and community, and it puts haggling first, ahead of trust.

Spoken, it is as warm as Jarak and works for both genders. But in writing every Syrian has seen «جاري التحميل…» thousands of times, so the logo reads as 'loading', and it would literally appear under the app's own spinner.

«لقيت شاري» and «كل شي إلو شاري» are warm and reassuring for sellers. But it is a generic word that appears in every listing, so it is hard to find as a brand. The Latin form reads as 'Sharia' or «شرعي» to returnees and minority users.

Thanks to Bab al-Hara it is warmer and more nostalgic to ordinary Syrians than the dossier score suggests, and mothers and older users would like it. But it sounds folksy and old-city to students, «حارتنا» can mean 'our side' in divided cities like Homs, and an existing app called Hartna already uses the name.

It is affectionate and street-smart, and the بسطة image fits second-hand goods. But it means a professional trader and suggests بالة and illegal pavement stalls being cleared away, so people selling cars or phones would find it cheap. Some will also hear بوسطجي (postman).

It is a friendly shopkeeper word («شو بدّك؟»), but intonation decides whether it sounds warm or rude, and the east says تريد. As a grammatical word it disappears in conversation, and «شفتها على بدّك» sounds odd.
Everyone understands it and it sounds playful, but a بازارجي is a wheeler-dealer, the very middleman type users want to avoid. بازار الشام and Auto Bazar already use the same root in Syria.

It is a lively souq phrase that people would smile at, but it is three words with a خ, it sounds Damascene to the east, and it suggests barter or tit-for-tat. It makes a good campaign line but is hard to say as a brand («نزّلتها على هات وخود»).

It is a catchy, Doushesh-like rhyme, but young, Kurdish and eastern users mostly won't know its 'cash on the spot' meaning. Those who do know it may hear 'empty talk', and its jokey tone undercuts trust for big-ticket items.
It is easy to say and spell, but to Syrians it means a nano-SIM or 'tiny'. It gives no idea of a market, neighbours or trust, and it feels foreign and a bit cheap for an Arabic-first app.
Syrians say بدّل, not the MSA بادل, and they will increasingly read «بادل» as the sport padel. It also signals swap-only, while the app is mainly cash sales.
Every Syrian knows «مضمون» from smuggler, visa and get-rich ads («تهريب مضمون»), and it promises a guarantee the app cannot give. After the first bad deal, «قالوا مضمون!» lands on the brand.

It is a beloved national image, but it belongs to Hama, it carries the melancholy 'groaning' and round-and-round sense, and it has nothing to do with buying and selling. The user's spelling نعورا also looks like a typo.

It is a warm closing blessing that all communities say, but as a brand the word حلال makes the returnee think of halal food and some minority users of religious framing. The Latin form needs Arabizi digits.

It sounds like a bank or ministry rather than a neighbour, it is said four different ways (mawsū', mawthūq...), and Gulf Syrians know it as a Saudi licence. It is far better used as a verified-store badge than as the brand.

To ordinary Syrians it means 'the deposit you hand over', which is exactly the scam step the app tells people never to take. That makes it a reputational liability despite the warm «عربون محبة» sense.
It is bookish school and news Arabic linked to crisis barter and political trade-offs, it is hard to say (ق and ض), and it falsely tells users the app is swap-only.
It is a delivery-app slogan rather than a name, it is long and lost among dozens of سوق apps, and to Syrian men «سَوقك» can also echo the military call-up («سوقك ع العسكرية»).

judges.top_pick_reasoning:
From the Syrian user's side, جارك is the only name that does three things at once. First, it says how the app works: the item is near you, you deal with a real person, and nobody sits in the middle. Second, it carries a proverb every Syrian already trusts («جارك القريب ولا خيّك البعيد», «الجار قبل الدار»), which answers the main complaint about chaotic Facebook and Telegram groups with no trust signals. Third, it is easy to pass on: «اسأل جارك», «فوت على جارك», «نزّلها على جارك».

It is everyday Arabic in every region (zh in Aleppo and Damascus, j in Deir ez-Zor and Hauran), Kurdish Arabic speakers understand it, and it has no religious, sectarian or single-city colour, because the neighbour is a shared value for Muslims, Christians and Druze. In Arabic script it reads for both genders (jārak or jārik), so the women users in an Arabic-first app see no masculine bias. It avoids every ق/ع/ح problem, and its tone is warm without being folksy (unlike حارتنا), formal (unlike موثوق) or cheap (unlike بسطجي).

Its weaknesses are real but secondary for a Syria-only app. The Latin 'Jarak' read by German speakers gives the vulgar Turkish-German 'yarak', so test it with returnees and give the Latin logo an Arabic-led look. The neighbour root is getting crowded (Jiran, Jeeran, Hartna). And a live Play, App Store and DCIP trademark search is still needed before filing.

مزبوط is a close second, and the better pick if the team wants a cheekier, more modern voice. It falls short because it says nothing about 'nearby', and as a common filler word it often won't be heard as a brand name in conversation.
judges.combos:
1) Main set: brand جارك (Jarak), with the trust words used as product labels rather than the name.
- Verified-store badge «موثوق ✓» («متجر موثوق»), given only to shops the staff have checked, so the claim is true. Because the brand is not موثوق, the badge does not suggest that every other seller is untrusted.
- Do not use «مضمون» as a badge. It suggests a warranty or escrow the platform does not give, and Syrians link it to smuggler and get-rich ads.

2) Tagline options for جارك:
- «جارك القريب… ولا سوق بعيد» (the proverb twist), or
- «بيع وشرا مزبوط… من جارك» (puts مزبوط in the tagline).

3) Using other words from the list inside the app:
- Post button: «نزّل إعلانك» (نزّل as the call to action, not the brand).
- Report entry: «شي مو مزبوط؟ بلّغ».
- Chat quick reply: «قدّيش آخر سعر؟».
- After a sale: «مبروك… حلال عليك».
- Safety tip on every listing: «لا تدفع عربون قبل ما تشوف الغرض بعينك».
- Seller campaign: «كل غرض إلو شاري».
- Outdoor or social campaign lines: «هات وخود… بلا وسيط» and «إيد بإيد، شندي بندي».

4) If مزبوط is the brand instead:
- Tagline «مزبوط… وقريب منك» or «اسأل جارك، على مزبوط».
- Same «موثوق ✓» badge for verified stores.
- Report button becomes the brand joke «مو مزبوط؟ بلّغنا».

ranking.reason: Suggestive, not descriptive. It hints at local, direct, trusted trade without naming classifieds, so it should clear Law 8/2007's bar on descriptive marks. It breaks completely with the سوق/حراج/بازار naming of ~35 rivals, and no classifieds app uses it (search-level evidence). Weak points: a masculine fixed form, the German 'Yarak' echo, and an Indonesian homonym that only adds Latin search noise. File Jarak and Jaarak defensively.

Distinctive in this category, with a clean conflict record and a single Latin wordmark (Mazboot) that sits apart from Turkish 'mazbut'. It is laudatory, though, so protection is moderate. Arabic search splits across مزبوط/مضبوط/مظبوط, and rivals can use «مضبوط» descriptively. A strong second choice, and even stronger as a tagline word.

I score it above the dossier. Apart from Naoura it is the only near-arbitrary mark here, and store search for it is easy to own. Doushesh's 200K downloads show a playful, opaque name can work in Syria. Against it: two words with spacing variants, an identical-name YouTube channel, an uncertain meaning (cash in hand vs. empty talk), and the French 'bandit' homophone.

Suggestive and memorable, with no classifieds conflict. But spelling splits badly. In Arabic it is قدّيش vs أدّيش. In Latin it is Addeish, Addesh or 2adesh, and the .sy domain is held under Addeish, not the better Addesh. Store search is also crowded by price and currency-rate queries ('قديش الدولار').

Arbitrary for classifieds, so legally the strongest category, and the wheel makes an excellent icon. The user's spelling نعورا is non-standard, and Latin spellings scatter. In Lebanon it collides with Naqoura, which hurts regional expansion, and Hama businesses already use the word freely.

Legally registrable, but Arabic store and in-app search would drown in «جاري التحميل/البحث». In Latin it is a common first name and one letter short of Jarir, the big Gulf phone retailer. Weak findability and enforcement. Jarak gives the same neighbour story without these problems.

The coined occupational form protects the exact word, but the بسطة root is already used by an App Store classifieds app (serious) and several Bastah/Bastaat apps. It also invites the بوسطجي/postman mishearing, and Europeans read 'Basta!' as 'enough!'.

The cleanest spelling on the list, but the mark is laudatory. The identical name is already used by an Arabic classifieds app, Jordan's MaksabJo marketplace and an Omani government marketplace. A Syrian filing might succeed, but store confusion and blocked regional expansion make it a poor asset.

It names the core action (post or download), so a plain word mark in Classes 9/35 risks refusal as descriptive of intended purpose. In the store it reads as a downloader utility. Better used as the primary call-to-action than as the brand.

Registrable as suggestive, but it is among the most frequent words in Levantine speech, so it cannot be owned in search and protection would be narrow. Search noise from the Turkish card game Batak, the English 'bad' first syllable and the masculine Latin form add to the problem.

'Buyer' names a party to every transaction, so it is near-generic and cannot be owned in search. In Latin it reads as Sharia/shar3i. Morocco's well-funded, licensed Chari (شاري) blocks regional scale.

The core 'bazar' is generic and already used by Syrian rivals Bazar AlSham and Auto Bazar, so it would look like one more look-alike. pazarji.co already uses the identical Arabic name. Protection would be narrow.
A three-word mark with a dozen-plus Latin spellings, buried under 'hat' results. The store title takes all 30 characters. Its distinctiveness rests on the logo, so it works better as a campaign line.

Diluted. An existing neighbourhood app with local ads (Hartna - حارتنا) already holds the name, and it is common for Facebook groups and shops. The ح spelling scatters, so ownership would be contested.

Arbitrary on paper, but one of the most diluted tokens in tech: Gemini Nano on Android, the Nano crypto coin, Ledger Nano, iPod nano. It is also descriptive of small size in Class 9. Store discoverability would be close to zero.

Laudatory, and arguably deceptive for a platform that guarantees nothing. It is a generic trust word inside listings and the signature word of scam and smuggler ads. That raises both refusal risk and liability.

Descriptive, verging on deceptive (the app takes no deposits). A same-name عربون app from a developer tied to a Syrian classifieds publisher is a serious conflict. Every deposit scam would become a story about the brand.

Laudatory, and held by the Saudi government Mawthooq licence. A same-category «سوق موثوق» app exists, and Syrian rival Haraj Syria already uses the word in its store copy. It cannot be enforced as a word mark, and it is better used as a badge word.
Blocked. An identical-name 'Badel' swap/sell marketplace has been live on Play and the App Store since 2024. Arabic search for «بادل» is also flooded by the sport padel.
Generic for barter services, so unregistrable as the type of service. It has more than ten Latin spellings, a «سوق المقايضة» app already exists, and it misdescribes a cash marketplace.

The Latin 'Halal' is generic and floods search with food, certification and Gulf livestock-classifieds apps named حلال. Several MENA offices may object to marks with religious significance (not verified for Syria). The name also needs Arabizi digits.

A descriptive slogan built on the سوق root, which at least 14 Syria-facing apps already share, so it is the exact look-alike pattern to escape. It implies delivery, has about 36 Latin spelling combinations, and is unregistrable as words.

judges.top_pick_reasoning: I judged this as a brand strategist and IP lawyer. Jarak is the only candidate that combines four things: (1) it is suggestive rather than descriptive or laudatory, so it should pass Law 8/2007's bar on signs that describe the service, its type or its quality; (2) there is no known same-category conflict (only minor delivery and gaming look-alikes, plus the Jiran/Jeeran neighbourhood root); (3) it breaks cleanly with the سوق/حراج/بازار/Syria naming used by about 35 rivals and from OpenSooq and Doushesh, so it is easy to tell apart in the store and to defend; (4) it has one stable Arabic spelling and one main Latin spelling. It also scales well. 'Your neighbour' works for any category, including cars and property later. It reads the same in Lebanon, Jordan, the Gulf and Iraq, and as Garak in Egypt. Its proverb story («جارك القريب ولا خيّك البعيد») backs the product's no-middleman, nearby, trust message without making a legal promise. Mazboot, the runner-up, is laudatory, and its search splits across three Arabic spellings. Remaining risks: the German 'Yarak' vulgar echo (it matters only for diaspora marketing, and the Arabic-first store title keeps it out of view in Syria), Indonesian 'jarak' Latin search noise outside Syria, and the masculine form (use جارتك/feminine copy in-app). Action plan for first-to-file: file now at the Directorate of Commercial and Industrial Property Protection as an Arabic plus Latin composite (جارك + Jarak), with Jaarak as a defensive Latin filing, in Classes 35, 9 and 42 (consider 38). Reserve Jarak and Jaarak handles and keep the matching .sy domains. Later, add Madrid designations or national filings when expanding. Caveat: I could not run fresh searches this turn (the shared web-search budget was used up). Every conflict judgement rests on the dossiers' search-level evidence, so Google Play, the App Store and the Syrian register must be checked live for جارك/Jarak/Jaarak before filing.
judges.combos:
Main recommendation: brand «جارك – Jarak», store title «جارك – Jarak | مستعمل قريب منك» (about 30 characters). Use «مزبوط» as the tagline and quality word, not as a second mark: «جارك… بيع وشرا مزبوط» or «من جارك، وبسعر مزبوط».

Trust badges (UI labels, not trademarks, and never filed as part of the mark): use «متجر موثّق» (muwaththaq, verified) for the staff-checked trusted-shop badge. It states a fact staff checked rather than a promise. Use «موثوق» only if a public criteria page backs it, and keep it visually distinct from «موثّق». Never use «مضمون» as a badge or label: it implies a guarantee or escrow the app does not give, which creates liability and complaints.

Microcopy that reuses the other names well: «نزّل إعلانك» as the main post button (Nazzel as a verb, not a brand); «قدّيش؟» as a quick-reply chip in buyer contact; «بسطتك» as the name of a seller's profile or storefront page; «مبروك، حلال عليك» as the Arabic-only message after a sale; «قابل للبدل» as a filter tag (better than مقايضة/بادل); «كل غرض إلو شاري» as the seller-acquisition campaign line; «إيد بإيد، شندي بندي، بلا وسيط» or «هات وخود… بلا وسيط» as pay-in-person campaign lines; «لا تدفع عربون قبل ما تشوف الغرض» as standing anti-scam safety copy.

Fallback if Jarak fails clearance: «مزبوط – Mazboot» with the tagline «من جارك وقريب منك» and the same «متجر موثّق» badge. Second fallback: «شندي بندي» if a user survey confirms the cash-in-hand meaning.

ranking.reason: This name fits the product best: a known person close by, dealing directly, with no middleman. It also claims nothing about vetting, so a 'my neighbour scammed me' story does not break a promise the way a trust word would. The risks can be managed: the Latin ending is masculine, the German reading 'Yarak' is a vulgar echo (but only diaspora readers would hear it, since login needs a +963 number), and a 'neighbour' brand needs safety copy that pushes meeting in public places.

It is warm and pan-Syrian and easy to register, and its promise ('done right') is soft rather than a guarantee. But every bad deal becomes «مو مزبوط». The formal spelling مضبوط also calls up police seizures (مضبوطات), which is a poor echo for a market already worried about stolen phones.

It has the same neighbour fit as Jarak, it is gender-neutral, and its foreign readings are harmless. But the app's own interface will show «جاري التحميل…» under the logo, «الحساب الجاري» hints at banking the app does not offer, and the word cannot be owned in Arabic search.

It names the core action (posting an ad) and promises no trust, so scams cannot be used against it. As a trademark, though, it is close to descriptive under Law 8/2007, it reads as 'download' in the app stores, it primes buyers to ask for a lower price, and it carries an unverified vulgar joke among teenagers.

It is clean to say, but 'profit' sounds trader-centric in an economy where people sell their belongings out of need, and it echoes 'win a prize' promotions that scammers use. An Arabic classifieds app with the identical name already exists, along with Jordan's MaksabJo and an Omani government Maksab, which is a real conflict risk for an investor.

It is playful and promises nothing, but it puts haggling and price first, and it is the same one-word comment sellers find annoying in Facebook groups. The 'how much?' word is also the naming device of currency-rate apps, so users may expect a dollar tracker. The ق/ʔ/q split is a regional and communal marker.

It makes no false promise, but in print its tone cannot be controlled: «شو بدّك؟!» can be rude, and «بدّك قتلة؟» is a threat. It reads as western Syrian, its Latin form starts with 'bad', and as a noun it is unusable in speech («شفتها على بدّك»).

It speaks only to buyers and is near-generic. Its Latin form can be read as 'Sharia' or as shar3i/«الشرعي», the title of a faction's religious official in recent Syrian usage, which is a political liability in today's climate. Morocco's Chari (شاري) fintech already holds the Arabic name.

The 'cash in hand' sense actually matches how deals here are settled, but it rests on thin evidence. The better-documented Levantine sense is 'empty talk', and the French reading 'bandit' is a poor fit for a trust brand. It feels too jokey for car listings, and younger and eastern users may not know it.

ranking.name_latin: Hat w Khod (user: Hay w khod)
ranking.reason: It suggests swapping and haggling, «علاقة هات وخود» makes it sound transactional, and 'give first' can be heard as 'pay first'. It is three words with خ, and the Latin form is buried under results for 'hat'. Use it as a campaign line, not as the brand.

Damascus is clearing unlicensed street stalls right now, so the word sits in the news as illegal encroachment. It also connotes بالة and cheap goods, names a professional street trader rather than a neighbour, and can be misheard as بوسطجي (postman), which suggests delivery.

It has nothing to do with the product and means 'tiny' or 'cheap'. The Nano coin and Ledger Nano wallets could lead users in a scam-prone market to think the app handles payments. It is also one of the most crowded tokens in tech, Gemini Nano on Android included.

A بازارجي is a dealer or flipper, the exact middleman the 'no middleman' promise is meant to remove, and the ـجي suffix can sound pejorative. The بازار root is already used by Syrian rivals (Bazar AlSham, Auto Bazar), and pazarji.co uses the identical name.

It promises a strictly hyperlocal service to a product that searches up to 200 km, and it reads as Damascus and Bab al-Hara with a working-class tint. In cities divided by community, 'our lane' can mean 'our side', and «حارة كل مين إيدو إلو» is ready-made mockery. An app called Hartna already exists.
It says 'swap' to a cash marketplace, and «بادل» is now the standard Arabic word for padel. An identical-name swap/buy/sell app (Egypt and Saudi Arabia, since 2024) blocks it.

It is the symbol of one city, Hama, which also carries the memory of 1982. In Latin it merges with Naqoura, the Lebanese border town known for war and ceasefire news. Its idiom («متل الناعورة») means going round in circles, the opposite of posting in under a minute.

It promises trust the app cannot vet, since anyone with a +963 number can post, so the first scam headline writes itself («موثوق؟!»). It also clashes with the planned «متجر موثّق» badge by implying the other sellers are not trusted. A Saudi government licence and a same-category «سوق موثوق» app already hold the word.

It tells users and store reviewers this is a barter-only app. In Syrian news the word means political and territorial trade-offs and crisis-economy barter. With both ق and ض it has no single spelling that matches how most Syrians say it.

'Guaranteed' implies a warranty or escrow the platform does not provide, so every faulty phone becomes «قالوا مضمون!» and a liability story. It is also stock vocabulary in smuggler and scam ads («تهريب مضمون», «ربح مضمون») and risks being refused as a deceptive mark.

The core word is an Islamic-law category. In today's sectarian climate, and in Latin script for the diaspora, the brand can read as religiously aligned or as a halal-food label. It collides with Gulf livestock apps called حلال and invites «حرام عليك» whenever a deal goes wrong.

It is a delivery slogan for an app that does not deliver. It is descriptive and lost in a crowd of سوق apps, it cannot be spelled one way in Latin, and سَوقك can echo conscription ('your call-up at your home').

This is the worst product fit on the list. The brand would literally be named 'Deposit', which normalises the most common classifieds scam (pay before you see the item) that the app's safety advice exists to stop. It also brings in the real-estate broker's «عقد عربون», a disputed fiqh topic, and a same-name Syrian-linked app.

judges.top_pick_reasoning: Seen through risk and product fit, Jarak is the only name that describes how the product actually works without promising anything the product cannot deliver. A neighbour is a person nearby, you deal with them directly, and there is no middleman. The name does not say 'trusted' (موثوق), 'guaranteed' (مضمون), 'deposit' (عربون), 'barter' (مقايضة/بادل), 'delivery' (سوقك ببيتك) or 'dealer' (بازارجي/بسطجي). So when a scam happens, the headline is 'someone lied on Jarak', not 'the trusted app lied', and the platform's reporting, moderation and verified-store tools tell the trust story instead of the brand. It has no political, religious, sectarian or single-city meaning, the neighbour is a value shared across Muslim, Christian and Druze communities, and it is understood the same way in every region. The risks I would carry into launch: (1) The German reading 'Yarak' is a vulgar Turkish echo. Login requires a +963 number, so few in-market users will hear it, but diaspora press and social media could mock it. Lead with the Arabic wordmark جارك, keep the Latin form small, and register Jaarak as well. (2) The Latin ending is masculine. Use جارتك in in-app copy and test the name with women. (3) A neighbour brand can tempt users to meet at home or share exact locations. Default safety copy should say «التقوا بمكان عام», and the app should keep location coarse and hide phone numbers. (4) Some may fear 'my neighbours will see me selling out of need', and it is worth testing in places where neighbour relations broke down during the conflict (the coast, Suwayda). (5) The conflict check rests on searches from 9 October and is not a clearance. Run live Play, App Store and Syrian trademark-register searches before filing, then file early as an Arabic plus Latin composite mark in classes 35, 9 and 42, because Syria is first-to-file. I rank Mazboot second: its promise is softer than Mawthouq's but it is still a promise that a bad deal turns into «مو مزبوط», and مضبوط echoes police seizures. Jari shares Jarak's fit but collides with «جاري التحميل» on every loading screen. Nazzel carries no promise risk but is too descriptive to defend as a trademark.
judges.combos: 1) Brand جارك, with a two-tier seller label. Private sellers show as «جار» or «جارك», and shops show the badge «متجر موثّق» (verified store). Use موثّق, not موثوق: 'verified' describes a check the staff actually did, while 'trusted' is a judgment the platform cannot stand behind. Never use «مضمون» anywhere, as badge or copy: it implies a guarantee, warranty or escrow, which creates liability, and it is scam-ad vocabulary. 2) Use «نزّل» as the main button and in the posting campaign: «نزّل إعلانك بدقيقة… والمشتري جنبك», or «نزّلها على جارك». It names the core action without having to defend a weak trademark. 3) Use «مزبوط» as the reporting hook rather than a brand claim: «شي مو مزبوط؟ بلّغ». This turns the mockery risk into a safety habit. 4) Use «عربون» only in a safety warning: «لا تدفع عربون قبل ما تشوف الغرض», which turns the worst brand candidate into the most useful line of trust-and-safety copy. 5) Show «مبروك، حلال عليك» in Arabic only, on the screen after a sale is marked done. It is warm, used by every community, and harmless in-app, but never put it in the brand or the Latin store title. 6) Campaign lines that need no badge: «جارك القريب… ولا سوق بعيد» (keep it about distance, not vetting), «كل غرض إلو شاري», and «إيد بإيد، بلا وسيط». 7) Store title (exactly 30 characters): «جارك – Jarak | مستعمل قريب منك». Fallback pairing if Jarak fails clearance: brand مزبوط, badge «متجر موثّق», and «نزّل إعلانك» as the call to action.

dossiers.meaning_literal: "Your neighbour" (said to a man): جار + ـك.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Everyday in every Syrian dialect and in Standard Arabic; warm and neutral, neither old-fashioned nor slangy. dossiers.meaning_literal: 'Correct, exactly right, accurate, properly done, OK'. It is the colloquial spelling of Standard Arabic مضبوط ('adjusted, precise'). Egyptians write it مظبوط.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Very common, warm and informal Levantine (Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine) and Egyptian dialect. It is neither old-fashioned nor formal. Uses: «مزبوط!» ('exactly!'), the question tag «مزبوط؟» ('right?'), «الحساب مزبوط» ('the bill is right'), «الوزن مزبوط» ('the weight is right'), and «شغلو مزبوط» ('his work is solid'). «زلمة مزبوط» probably means 'a proper, decent guy' (unverified). The same root gives the trade verb «زبطت» ('it worked out', as in «زبطت البيعة», 'the sale went through') and «بيزبط هيك؟» ('does this price work?'). So the word sits right in the language of closing a fair deal (unverified dialect knowledge, needs native checks). In Egypt «قهوة مظبوط» is medium-sweet coffee; Syrians usually say «وسط» (unverified). Gulf speakers understand it from Egyptian and Levantine media but use «تمام/زين» more. Iraqis know «مضبوط». It is understood in the east and in Kurdish areas, where people may prefer «زين» (unverified). In formal written Arabic, the spelling مضبوط also means 'seized / caught (by police)': «تم ضبط», «المضبوطات».
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: ط (emphatic t) is one of the penalised letters, but in Latin it is simply 't' (the Arabizi '6' is rare). The bigger issue is the Arabic spelling split: مزبوط (Levantine as spoken), مضبوط (Standard Arabic) and مظبوط (Egyptian). Users will search all three. City speakers say [mazˤbuːtˤ], while some eastern and Bedouin speakers may say [maðˤbuːtˤ] ('mathboot'). Everyone understands it, with a small difference in sound. Latin vowels split between oo, ou and u: Mazboot (English style), Mazbout (French style), and Mazbut, which is also the Turkish spelling. The Oct 9 notes already flagged Mazboot, Mazbout and Mazbut. Best spelling: 'Mazboot'. English readers say it right ('maz-BOOT'), and it differs from the Turkish word. Register Mazbout and Mazbut too, and add مضبوط and مظبوط as store keywords.

dossiers.meaning_literal: Two readings with the same Arabic letters. (1) جاري jāri, "my neighbour". (2) جارٍ/جاري jārī, "running, ongoing, current", the participle of جرى.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: In speech, "my neighbour" is everyday in every dialect («جاري أبو محمد», «يا جاري») and is warm and neutral. dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: ج is [ʒ] in Damascus, Aleppo, Homs, Hama and the coast; [dʒ] in the east, among Bedouin and in Hauran; and [g] in Egypt. Every variant fits under 'J' except Egyptian 'Gari'. ر and ي pose no problem, and no Arabizi digits are needed. German speakers will say 'Yari'. French speakers say [ʒaʁi], which is close to the Damascene sound. Two syllables, one obvious Latin spelling. Best: Jari.

dossiers.meaning_literal: Imperative of the verb نزّل: "bring it down / put it down / lower it". By extension it means post or upload, download, lower the price, and unload.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: It is both Standard Arabic and dialect, used every day in every Syrian region and across the Arab world. The senses Syrians actually use: (1) Posting online: «نزّل بوست/صورة/إعلان», «نزّلت الإعلان عالفيسبوك». This is exactly the app's core action, and the earlier notes list «نزّل إعلانك ببلاش» ("post your ad for free") as natural copy. (2) Downloading: «نزّل التطبيق» (تنزيل = download), which is handy for install ads. (3) Lowering a price: «نزّللي شوي», «نزّل من السعر» are standard haggling lines, and «تنزيلات» on shop windows means sales or discounts. (4) Unloading goods, or a passenger telling a microbus driver «نزّلني هون» ("drop me here"). The register is neutral and practical, and the bare imperative is a little punchy and playful. It has no regional colour: Damascus, Aleppo, Homs, the coast, Deir ez-Zor, Hauran/Suwayda, Idlib and the Kurdish areas say it the same way, apart from the vowel (nazzel or nazzil). Gulf, Egyptian, Lebanese and Iraqi speakers read it the same way too. It is a masculine imperative (to a woman: نزّلي), but Arabic app buttons normally use the masculine imperative for everyone (حمّل، سجّل), so this is less awkward than the ending of جارك. "Nazzel" is a correct spelling, not a typo. It matches the Damascene vowel; "Nazzil" is the Standard Arabic, Lebanese and Gulf vowel.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Letters ن ز ل plus a shadda. None of the problem letters appear and no Arabizi digits are needed. ز is pronounced /z/ everywhere, so the consonants are stable across Syria. The variation is in the second vowel (e in Damascus, i in Aleppo, Lebanon, the Gulf and Standard Arabic) and in whether the double z is written (many people will type "Nazel" or "Nazil"). In Arabic many users will type نزل without the shadda, which is fine but collides with نُزُل (inn) and نزل (he went down). People would type Nazzel, Nazzil, Nazel or Nazil. The best single spelling is "Nazzel": it keeps the doubling and the Syrian vowel. Register Nazzil, Nazel and Nazil as defensive handles and keywords.
dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: it sounds close to "nozzle" or "nasal", which is harmless and slightly comic. Nothing vulgar. German: z is read /ts/, so it comes out as "NAT-sel". The first three letters, N-A-Z, also look like "Nazi". The risk is low, but a German-speaking diaspora check is advisable, and the logo should not stress "NAZ". French: faintly evokes the slang "naze/nase" ("rubbish, knackered"), a weak link. Turkish: "nâzil" (Ottoman/religious register) means "descended, revealed", and "nazlı" (coy, spoiled; also a girl's name) is a positive sound-alike. Persian: نازل (nāzel) means "low/cheap" of prices, which actually suits a bargain marketplace. Kurdish/Persian/Turkish "naz" means coquetry or charm, which is positive. No embarrassing foreign meaning was found.
dossiers.sensitivities: Religious echo: in Standard Arabic, نزّل with God as subject is the language of revelation (نَزَّلَ الكتاب، نَزَّلنا الذِّكر), and تنزيل is a Quranic term for revelation. In everyday Syrian use nobody hears this; ads that say «نزّل إعلانك» are the ordinary sense. The risk is very low, but avoid copy that echoes Quranic phrasing (e.g. «تنزيل…» headlines). Crude slang: نزل/نزّل (from the jurists' term إنزال) can refer to ejaculation in vulgar talk. Normal phrases are unaffected, but teenagers can joke with the bare imperative «نزّل!». This is the researcher's knowledge and needs a native check. Product fit: the "lower the price" sense can prime buyers to make lowball offers. Haggling is normal in Syrian person-to-person sales and does not contradict the no-middleman, no-deposit model, so it can be played as a joke («نزّل إعلانك… مش السعر»). No political, sectarian, single-city or class/poverty meaning. «تنزيلات» (sales) is a positive association.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Descriptive, leaning suggestive. The verb names the user's main action: post an ad, and download the app. Under Syria's Law 8/2007 bar on signs that describe a characteristic or intended purpose (وجهة الاستعمال) of the service, a plain word mark in Classes 35/9 could be refused or would be weak. File a composite mark (logo + «نزّل NAZZEL»). Even then, rivals can still use «نزّل إعلانك» in their own copy.
dossiers.tagline_en: "Post your ad in a minute… the buyer is right next to you."

key_claims.claim: The project's search-level check (Oct 2026) found no app named Nazzel/نزّل, and the second report ranked it 5th on the combined shortlist. No fresh Arabic or Latin search could be run today because the web-search budget was used up and direct fetches were blocked.
In Syrian and Levantine copy, نزّل is the natural verb for posting an ad («نزّل إعلانك ببلاش»). It also means download and lower the price.

The Form II verb نزّل appears in Quranic verses about revelation (e.g. 3:3 «نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ», 15:9 «إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ», 25:1 «تَبَارَكَ الَّذِي نَزَّلَ الْفُرْقَانَ»), so it has a faint religious register in Standard Arabic.

Syria's Law 8/2007 says signs that may indicate a characteristic of the product or service (type, quality, quantity, intended purpose/وجهة الاستعمال, value) are not distinctive marks. That is a risk for a verb naming the core action of an ad-posting service.
Syria is first-to-file, and Latin marks need an Arabic translation or transliteration, so «نزّل NAZZEL» should be filed together, before launch.
Foreign readings: Persian نازل = low/cheap (of prices); Turkish nâzil = descended/revealed; French slang naze = rubbish; German readers pronounce z as /ts/.
Vulgar slang: نزل/نزّل can mean ejaculate (from the jurists' term إنزال). The risk is low because the neutral senses dominate everyday use.
Arabic store search for نزل/نزّل is likely to be noisy, because many download-tool apps use تنزيل/نزّل in their titles.

dossiers.verdict_reason: Of these three it has the best meaning fit. It is the exact action of «post in under a minute», it doubles as «download the app», and it hints at «تنزيلات» bargains. It is also truly pan-Syrian and pan-Arab, with no regional, class or sectarian colour, and no same-name app was found. The weaknesses are manageable but real. It is a descriptive verb (file as a composite mark with a distinctive logo), the Latin spelling drifts (Nazzel/Nazzil/Nazel), Arabic search will be noisy, and two mild echoes (Quranic «نزّل», a crude slang sense) need native checks. Keep it only if a fresh Google Play, App Store and trademark check comes back clear.

dossiers.meaning_literal: Buyer (active participle of شرى 'to buy'; in Classical Arabic the root can also mean 'to sell').
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: An everyday Syrian and pan-Arab word, the same in dialect and MSA. Sellers say 'في شاري؟' (is there a buyer?) and 'لقيت شاري' (I found a buyer). Listings often address 'الشاري' directly (inference). The folk saying 'كل شي إلو شاري' (everything has its buyer) is reassuring for sellers but unverified as a fixed proverb. Idiomatic uses (unverified): 'شاري خاطرك' (I'm doing it to please you), and dismissive 'مين شاريك؟' (who even cares about you?). Understood equally in Damascus, Aleppo, the coast, Hauran and the east, and by Gulf, Egyptian and Iraqi speakers. In Moroccan Darija the same word underlies the funded start-up Chari (شاري). It is masculine; the feminine is شارية. The user's spelling is correct.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: No problem Arabic letters (ش ا ر ي) and the same sound everywhere. The Latin side is mostly clean: 'Shari'. Variants: Shary, Sharee, Shaari, and the French 'Chari' (which is what Morocco's Chari uses). The real Latin problem is Arabizi ambiguity. Without digits, 'shari' can also be read as شارع (street, 'shari3'), as شرعي (sharia-compliant/legitimate, 'shar3i'), or as 'Sharia'. Best single spelling: 'Shari'.

dossiers.sensitivities: Religious/historical: الشُّراة (singular الشاري, 'those who sold their souls to God') was the Kharijites' name for themselves. dossiers.meaning_literal: "How much?" Levantine dialect, from قدّ + إيش ("what amount"). Used for prices and quantities.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: An everyday spoken word that every western Syrian uses all the time. It is the first thing a buyer asks under a listing ("قدّيش؟", "قدّيش آخر سعر؟"). It is dialect, not MSA (MSA is كم / بكم), and sounds friendly and playful rather than formal. Learner guides write it as 'addeish' / 'A'desh'. How it is said varies by region. Damascus, Aleppo, Homs and Hama cities say 'addēsh with a glottal stop, and chat often writes it أدّيش / اديش / 2adesh. Suwayda (Druze), many coastal and rural villages, and Deir ez-Zor keep the q: qaddēsh. Hauran and Bedouin speakers say gaddēsh. The Mesopotamian-dialect east (Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa, Hasakah) mostly says بيش / شكد / كم, though people there know قدّيش from Damascene TV. Kurdish speakers say 'bi çiqas?' in Kurmanji but understand the Arabic. Outside Syria: Lebanese, Jordanians and Palestinians use قدّيش / أدّيه. Gulf Arabs (بكم) and Egyptians (بكام) recognise it as Shami. Iraqis say بيش / شكد. Turkish speakers do not know it. The user's 'Addeish' is a real learner-guide spelling, not a typo, but it is not how Syrians type the word.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Two problems. (1) It starts with ق, the letter with the worst regional split in Syria: ʔ in the cities, q among Druze, coastal and Deir speakers, g in Hauran and Bedouin speech. Any Latin spelling picks a side. 'A-' spellings sound urban Damascus/Aleppo; Q- and K- spellings sound rural or Classical. Even the Arabic is split between قدّيش (the written-dialect form) and أدّيش (the city chat form). (2) The Latin forms scatter: Addeish, Addesh, Adesh, 2adesh, 2desh, Qaddesh, Addaysh. Syrians most often type 'adesh' or '2adesh'. German readers say 'ei' as 'eye', so 'Addeish' comes out as 'Ad-daisch'. English readers may stress the first syllable (ADD-esh) instead of ad-DESH. Best single spelling: 'Addesh'. It avoids the German 'ei' trap, needs no digit, sits closest to what Syrians type, and does not collide with the Indian given name 'Adesh'. But the user's .sy domain is reportedly for 'Addeish', so addesh.sy (and adesh.sy) would need checking. Otherwise keep 'Addeish' and buy the variants. The word has no gender (no -ak/-ik split like Jaarak), which is a plus.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: reads as 'add' + '-ish' and may look like a typo. No negative meaning. German: 'Addeish' is read 'Ad-daisch' because ei = /aɪ/; 'Addesh' avoids this. No meaning. French: 'ei' is read as è, so 'a-dèsh' comes close to the Arabic. No meaning. Turkish: letters are read one by one ('ad-de-ish'). No meaning found. Spelling hazards: 'Qaddesh'/'Kaddesh' look like Kaddish, the Jewish mourner's prayer (Aramaic qaddīš, 'holy'). They also look like Kadesh, the Bronze-Age city and battle site at Tell Nebi Mend about 25 km SW of Homs (historical and neutral). 'Adesh/Aadesh' is an Indian given name meaning 'command/order' in Hindi/Sanskrit. No vulgar meaning found in English, German, French or Turkish.
dossiers.sensitivities: No political, religious or sectarian meaning in Arabic. The risks: (a) Regional coding. The word is Levantine/western-Syrian, and the Latin 'A-' spelling encodes urban Damascus/Aleppo speech. Eastern Syrians say بيش/شكد, so the name sounds slightly 'Shami' to them, though it does not belong to one city the way حارة or Hamidiyah do. (b) It foregrounds price and haggling. 'قدّيش؟' is also the stereotypical one-word comment sellers find annoying in Facebook sale groups (inference, not sourced). That fits a classifieds app but can feel cheap. It also slightly shadows the 'trust' and 'nearby' messages. (c) Only the Q/K Latin spellings carry the Kaddish association. No class, poverty or middleman meaning.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Suggestive. An everyday interrogative that hints at prices without describing classifieds services. Registrable and memorable, but rivals can still use the word freely in their copy.

It is the first question in every second-hand deal, it is playful and distinctive (suggestive mark), it has no gender, and no marketplace uses it. It loses points on rules this project already set. It starts with ق, so the Latin spelling (Addeish/Addesh/Adesh/2adesh/Qaddesh) and even the Arabic (قدّيش/أدّيش) split by region. It reads Levantine rather than eastern Syrian. As a question word it is awkward to use as a noun in speech ('نزّلتها على قدّيش' sounds like 'I posted it for how much?'). dossiers.meaning_literal: "You want" (said to one man; Levantine dialect). It comes from بِوِدّك, "it is your wish". It also means "you need to" or "you'll have to", as in بدّك تستنّى, "you'll have to wait".
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: This is dialect only, never Standard Arabic (where you would say تريد/تودّ). It is very common and very casual. Typical uses: «شو بدّك؟» ("what do you want / what can I get you?"), «بدّك ياه؟» ("do you want it?"), «إذا بدّك» ("if you like"), «متل ما بدّك» ("as you wish"). The tone depends entirely on intonation. A shopkeeper's «شو بدّك عمّو؟» is warm. A curt «شو بدّك؟!» means "what do you want from me?!", and it turns up in threats like «بدّك قتلة؟» ("do you want a beating?"). It is native in Damascus, Homs, Hama, the coast, Aleppo, Idlib and Hauran/Suwayda, with vowels that shift between baddak, biddak and beddak. In Raqqa and Bedouin speech بدّي is used next to ودّي. In Deir ez-Zor and Hasakah, whose dialect is close to Iraqi, the native verb is تريد ("shtirīd?"). Speakers there understand بدّك from Syrian TV, but it marks the speaker as western Syrian. Kurdish-area Arabic speakers and the diaspora understand it. Gulf speakers say تبي/تبغى, Egyptians عايز, Iraqis تريد; all of them recognise بدّك as Syrian/Levantine speech from TV drama. It means nothing to Turkish speakers. As a brand it speaks to the buyer ("whatever you want") and says nothing about selling, second-hand, nearby or trust. "Baddak" is a correct Syrian Latin-letter spelling, not a typo. Lebanese and Palestinian users would more often write "Biddak".
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Letters ب د ك plus a shadda. None of the problem letters (ق ع ح خ ث ض ط ص غ) appear and no Arabizi digits are needed, so there is no consonant split by region. The problems are vowels and gender. (1) The first vowel varies: baddak in most of Syria, biddak in Palestine/Jordan and parts of Lebanon, beddak in some coastal and rural speech. (2) The ending is masculine: a woman is told baddik/baddek. The Arabic spelling بدّك is the same for both genders, which helps, but the Latin "Baddak" fixes the masculine form. (3) The east uses تريد/ودّك instead. People would type Baddak, Badak, Biddak or Baddek. The best single spelling is "Baddak": it matches Syrian speech and the user's own spelling. Claim the "Biddak" and "Badak" handles defensively.

"batak kredi" is a bad loan and "batakhane" a gambling den, so Turkish ears may hear a mild negative (not checked with native speakers). Indonesian/Malay: "badak" means rhinoceros and "bedak" face powder; both harmless and irrelevant to Syria. That is not offensive in the east, but it is not how people there speak (they say تريد). The Latin form is masculine, the same problem as Jaarak. No class or poverty meaning, and nothing that contradicts the product (no middleman, haggling or deposit sense). One practical problem: it is a grammatical word, so as a noun in speech it sounds odd («شفتها على بدّك» = "I saw it on you-want"), and when someone says بدّك in conversation nobody hears a brand.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Suggestive. It hints at wanting or demand without describing classifieds services, so it should pass Syria's Law 8/2007 bar on descriptive signs. But it is one of the most common words in Levantine speech, so the scope of protection is narrow and the word cannot be owned in search.

dossiers.meaning_literal: بسطة (a street stall: goods spread on a cloth or table on the pavement) plus the job suffix ـجي. It means 'the stall guy', a street-stall seller.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: بسطة is everyday Syrian and Levantine speech for a pavement stall. Syrian press uses it for stalls selling بالة (second-hand clothes) and cheap goods, so the root fits second-hand trade very well. It sounds humble, honest and street-level. The form بسطجي is not documented in Syrian media. People more often say 'صاحب بسطة' or 'أبو البسطة' (unverified). It is still understood at once because ـجي is a productive suffix, and it has a jokey, affectionate tone ('صرت بسطجي'). Downsides: بسطات are linked to informal or illegal pavement selling. Damascus governorate ran removal campaigns in April and May 2025 and again in May 2026, and coverage frames stalls as 'إشغالات' (encroachments) and as a sign of poverty. The suffix can sound pejorative. Regional: the word works across Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and the Gulf (Saudi 'Bastaat' and UAE 'Bastah' apps use the same sense). In Beirut, al-Basta is a neighbourhood named after its stall vendors. dossiers.meaning_literal: 'Give (me) and take'. هات is the irregular imperative 'give me / bring'; خود is the Levantine imperative of أخد 'take' (MSA خُذ). The order is give-first.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Everyday Levantine dialect, informal and playful, with a souq-like ring. It is used for a direct hand-to-hand exchange or quid pro quo, as in «الدنيا هات وخود» ('life is give and take'). The MSA idiom is أخذ وعطاء / أخذ ورد (researcher knowledge, unverified; I found no dialect-dictionary source). The connotations cut both ways. It evokes direct person-to-person trade with nobody in between, which fits. But it also evokes back-and-forth haggling, and the give-first order can be heard as 'pay me first, then take it', which is the pattern of advance-payment scams in Syrian Facebook sale ads. Regionally, خود/هات is western-Syrian/Levantine. In the Mesopotamian east (Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah) people say خذ and often انطيني for 'give me' (Iraqi-like), so they understand it but it sounds Damascene/Western (likely). Egyptians say it in reverse, «خد وهات» (khod w hat), which can also mean a heated back-and-forth (unverified). Gulf speakers say خذ/عطني and will read it as Levantine. Both verbs are masculine singular imperatives; the feminine is هاتي وخدي. The user's 'Hay w khod' is almost certainly a typo for 'Hat w Khod': t and y are adjacent on a QWERTY keyboard, and 'Hay' would read as هاي 'this' or حيّ.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: There is one problem letter, خ. It sounds the same across Syria, but in Latin it is 'kh' in English, '5' in Arabizi, 'ch' for German speakers, 'x' in Kurdish Latin script and 'h' in Turkish. The conjunction و adds w/wa/we/o/u, and the vowel of خود adds khod/khud/khood/khoud. The Arabic spelling also splits three ways: هات وخود (Syrian), هات وخد (Egyptian/short) and هات وخذ (MSA-ish). It is a three-token name, so a dozen or more realistic Latin spellings exist, and store search will not unify them. Best spelling: 'Hat w Khod', no digits, as one wordmark (e.g. HatwKhod) or with a ⇄ device.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: 'Hat' is headwear, so the name reads like a hat shop at first glance (searches for the Latin form return only hat results), and 'Khod' looks like 'code/cod'. The user's typo 'Hay' would read as dried grass, or 'hey'. German: 'hat' = 'has' (er hat), so 'Hat w Khod' looks like broken German. Germans would spell خ as 'ch' (Chod). French: no meaning. 'Hat' is not a French word, and the h is silent for French readers ('at'). Turkish: 'hat' = line (phone line, transit route), a common neutral word. Turkish has no kh, so it would be typed 'Hat ve Hod'. Kurmanji Kurdish: 'hat' = 'came', from 'hatin' (unverified). No vulgar or embarrassing reading was found.
dossiers.sensitivities: No religious, sectarian or political charge, and no single-city tie, though the خود form sounds Western-Syrian to eastern Syrians. The product risks are in the meaning. (1) It suggests barter or swapping, while the app sells for cash. (2) The give-first order can be heard as 'pay first', which echoes the advance-payment and lure scams that Syrian Facebook sale ads are known for. (3) Back-and-forth haggling clashes with a calm, trust-first tone. (4) The masculine imperative addresses men by default, the same issue earlier research found with Jaarak. (5) A blunt «هات!» to a stranger can sound demanding. No class or poverty connotation.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Suggestive: a common idiom that evokes exchange without describing classifieds services. It is distinctive enough to register as an Arabic+Latin composite mark, but the phrase is everyday speech, so competitors can still use it descriptively in copy. Protection depends on the logo.

dossiers.meaning_literal: A rhyming reduplication (إتباع) with no literal Arabic root meaning. The main idiomatic sense is 'cash on the spot, paid hand to hand' (يدفع أو يستلم نقداً). A second recorded Levantine sense is 'this and that' or 'empty talk'. Proposed origins: Turkish 'şunda bunda' ('here and there') or 'şimdi bindi'. Both are disputed.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: It is a colloquial, old-fashioned and humorous expression known in Syria, Jordan and Egypt. An Arabic Q&A site gives the Syrian meaning as paying or receiving cash. Youm7 calls it an old popular expression for immediate cash payment. A Jordanian article uses it for paying cash up front. For a phone-to-phone, no-fee, no-deposit market where buyer and seller meet and settle in cash, the 'cash in hand, no strings' sense fits. A Levantine dialect essay (Saqr Abu Fakhr, al-Araby) lists it among reduplications for someone talking without substance ('شروي غروي'), which is a bad sense for a trust brand. Recognition is probably higher among older Syrians. Younger, Kurdish and eastern Syrians may not know it (not tested). To those listeners it would sound like a catchy nonsense rhyme, similar to how 'Doushesh' works. Egyptians know it (an old Ali al-Kassar play title is reported, unverified). Sudanese will think of the city of Shendi (شندي). Gulf speakers are unlikely to know it. The user's Latin spelling is fine, not a typo.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: All letters are easy: ش ن د ي ب ن د ي. There are no emphatic or guttural letters, no digits, and it sounds the same across Syrian regions. The issues are vowel quality (shandi, shendi or shindi; Egyptians write شندى بندى with alif maqsura) and the fact that it is two words. That gives spacing variants (ShandiBandi, Shandi-Bandi) and English 'Shandy Bandy'. Best spelling: 'Shandi Bandi', with a joined wordmark 'ShandiBandi' for handles.

dossiers.meaning_literal: "Nano": the metric prefix for one-billionth, from Greek nanos, "dwarf". Informally it means "tiny".
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: A foreign loanword, neither Standard Arabic nor dialect. Syrians know it from technology: «شريحة نانو» (nano-SIM), «تكنولوجيا النانو» (nanotechnology), the iPod nano, nano-ceramic car coatings and "nano" claims in shops. It is also used jokingly for something tiny (e.g. «قدّ النانو»; not verified). It may also sound like a baby or pet name (cf. Levantine نونو "baby", and نانا as a nickname). It sounds modern, techy, small, perhaps cheap. It is understood the same way in every Syrian region, the Gulf, Egypt, Iraq, Turkey and Europe. It says nothing about markets, second-hand goods, nearby sellers, direct contact or trust. At best it is a faint pun on "small ads" (the literal meaning of Kleinanzeigen) or on a light, fast app. The user's spelling is correct.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Letters ن ا ن و: no problem letters, no Arabizi digits, no regional split, and no gender ending. The Arabic spelling نانو is fixed, and the Latin "Nano" is fixed worldwide. English speakers say "NAN-oh", Arabic and most European speakers "NAA-no"; neither causes confusion. This is the cleanest pronunciation and spelling of the three. Best spelling: "Nano".

dossiers.meaning_literal: بازار (market or bazaar, a Persian word) plus the Ottoman-Turkish job suffix ـجي (-cı/-ci). So it means 'market man' or 'bazaar trader'. Ottoman Turkish had بازارجی (bazarcı, 'stallholder'), and modern Turkish has pazarcı (street-market vendor).
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Every Syrian knows بازار: in shop names (بازار الشام), charity sales (بازار خيري) and street speech. The ـجي suffix is still productive in Levantine speech (قهوجي, كندرجي, بوسطجي = postman, from Turkish post+ji), so بازارجي is understood at once. However, I found no Syrian media or dialect source that uses بازارجي as an everyday word. It is a clear coinage, not a common word. In the dialect the suffix often names a trade or a habit, and it can turn pejorative (عربجي = rough man, سكرجي = drunkard). An Aswan University study (2025) describes -ji shifting from honorific to pejorative in Egyptian Arabic. So بازارجي can sound like a wheeler-dealer or professional flipper who 'plays the market', not like a neighbour clearing out a sofa. Earlier project notes also flagged an unverified Levantine sense of بازار as haggling or horse-trading ('بدنا نعمل بازار'), and that sense pushes the same way. Regional readings: Aleppo and the north use more Turkish loanwords and will find it natural. Deir ez-Zor and the Iraqi-influenced east use -چي heavily, so it reads fine there. Kurds use 'bazar' for a market, so the root crosses into Kurdish. Gulf speakers prefer حراج or سوق and will find it a little foreign. Egyptians say 'bazargi', and in Egypt بازار suggests tourist and antique shops (unverified). Turks hear 'pazarcı', a market-stall seller. Register: colloquial, playful, a little old-souq.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: There are no ق ع ح خ ث ض ط ص غ and no Arabizi digits. The only regional split is ج. Damascus and Aleppo say /ʒ/ (zh), Bedouin, rural and eastern speakers say /dʒ/, and Egyptians say /g/, which gives 'Bazargi'. People will type Bazarji, Bazarjy, Bazarjee, Bazaarji (after the English spelling 'bazaar') and Pazarji. Turks read Latin 'j' as /ʒ/ and would spell it Pazarcı. Best single spelling: Bazarji (one 'a' after the z, as in Arabic and Kurdish).

German: 'Basar' means a charity or second-hand sale (Kinderbasar = used children's goods), which is a good fit for diaspora users in Germany. Germans read J as Y ('Basar-yi'), which is harmless. Adding -ji only describes 'a market trader', so the mark would get narrow protection and be easy to crowd.

dossiers.meaning_literal: 'Guaranteed, assured, a safe bet'. It is the passive participle of ضَمِنَ ('to guarantee, vouch for'). In Standard Arabic it also means 'content, substance' («مضمون الرسالة»).
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: An everyday word in both dialect and Standard Arabic, used and understood all over Syria. It means a sure thing: «مضمون مية بالمية», «هالشغلة مضمونة», «البضاعة مضمونة». In second-hand phone and car talk, «مضمون» is the seller's own promise that the item works. OpenSooq listings use it as a trust word. It is common in irony too: «ما في شي مضمون» ('nothing is guaranteed'). Other senses (unverified, need native checks): (1) in Lebanon, «المضمون» is the worker insured by the social security fund (NSSF); (2) in Levantine farming and trade, «ضمان» / «ضمّن» means leasing an orchard's crop or a shop for a fixed fee, so «مضمون» can mean 'leased out'. Gulf and Egyptian readers take it as 'guaranteed'. In Turkish, Persian and Urdu the cognate (mazmun / mazmoon) means 'theme, content, essay', so Turkish-speaking Syrians will not hear 'guaranteed'. It also appears in hype phrases such as «دخل مضمون» and «ربح مضمون» ('guaranteed income/profit'), which are typical of get-rich-quick and scam ads (inference, with one advertorial example).
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: ض is the problem letter. Most of Syria (Damascus, Aleppo, Homs, Hama, the coast, Hauran) and Egypt say an emphatic [dˤ]: 'madmūn'. Deir ez-Zor, Bedouin, Iraqi and Gulf speakers merge ض with ظ and say [ðˤ]: 'maḏmūn', typed Madhmoun or Mathmoun (likely, not checked for this word). Turkish, Persian and Urdu speakers say [z]: Mazmun. No Arabizi digit is needed, but writers choose between d, dh and D. The vowel splits into ou, oo and u (Madmoun, Madmoon, Madmun). The Arabic spelling is fixed. Best spelling: 'Madmoun'. Avoid 'Madmoon', which English readers see as 'Mad Moon'.

dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Every Syrian knows النواعير as Hama's emblem and a national heritage picture (postcards, schoolbooks, Hamwi pride). Positive, but it reads 'Hama'. The word is not used for trade. Its everyday metaphors run against the product: «متل الناعورة» means going round and round, or someone who talks or complains without stopping. The norias' creaking 'groan' (أنين النواعير) is a stock image of lament in poetry (own knowledge). The idea of goods 'circulating' as reuse is something the brand would have to teach. Elsewhere: Egyptians say ساقية; Iraqis know norias on the Euphrates (unverified); Lebanese hear 'Na'oura' as their pronunciation of الناقورة (Naqoura). On spelling: the user's Arabic «نعورا» is non-standard, apparently colloquial na'ūra with a final alif. It looks like a misspelling and will not match searches for ناعورة. Use ناعورة. The Latin 'Naoura' is a reasonable French-style spelling.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: ع sounds the same across Syria, but Latin has no letter for it. It is either dropped (Naoura, Naura) or written with the digit 3 (Na3oura). The Arabic itself splits: نعورا / ناعورة / ناعوره. The French-style 'ou' works for Levantine and French readers, but English readers may say 'Now-ra' and Germans 'Na-o-u-ra'. Three syllables and at least five Latin spellings. In Latin it also merges with Naqoura (الناقورة, said 'Na'oura' wherever ق is a glottal stop). Best spelling if kept: Naoura, with Arabic ناعورة.

dossiers.meaning_literal: The Form III verb بادَلَ, 'to exchange (with someone)'. The imperative بادِل (bādil/bādel) means 'Exchange!' / 'Swap!'.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Syrians understand it, but as MSA, not dialect. Everyday Syrian speech uses بدّل (baddel), تبديل, بدل and «للبدل» in ads. بادل itself mostly appears in fixed MSA phrases (بادله الشعور, تبادل) (researcher knowledge, unverified). More important: in today's Arabic across the Gulf, Egypt, Lebanon and now Syria, «بادل» is the standard spelling of the racket sport PADEL, because Arabic has no p (ملاعب البادل, رياضة البادل). SANA reported in June 2026 that padel had reached Latakia with its first court, so Syrians will increasingly read «بادل» as the sport. dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: No problem letters: ب ا د ل map cleanly, with no ق ع ح خ, no Arabizi digits, and the same consonants everywhere. The only wobble is the vowels: MSA bādil vs. Syrian bādel, and whether the long ā is written (Baadel). It is easily confused with the colloquial بدّل (Baddel) and with بدل (Badal). Turkish readers will map it to 'bedel'. Best spelling: 'Badel', which matches the existing app and the Syrian pronunciation.

dossiers.meaning_literal: Deposit / earnest money: an advance paid to reserve an item or bind a sale. If the buyer goes ahead it counts toward the price, and if they back out the seller keeps it. Also used figuratively for 'a token / pledge' (عربون محبة، عربون صداقة).
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Used the same way in MSA and in Syrian dialect, and understood everywhere in Syria and the Arab world. In everyday Syrian life it means the cash you hand over to hold a flat, car, wedding hall or appliance ('دفعت عربون'). It is a serious, money-and-contract word, a little old-fashioned in the figurative sense ('عربون محبة', a small token of affection, said warmly or ironically). Syrian civil law (Civil Code art. 104) treats a deposit as giving each side the right to withdraw, and court rulings on deposit disputes are common. Gulf, Egyptian, Iraqi and Jordanian speakers use the same word in the same sense. Classical forms include عَرَبون، عُرْبون، عُربان. The Latin 'Arboon' is a reasonable rendering, not a typo.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: It starts with ع, which has no Latin letter. Arabizi writes '3arboon', and plain Latin drops it ('Arboon'), which is common (cf. 'Amman', 'Arab') but loses the sound. Pronunciation is fairly uniform across Syria (ʿarbūn; some say ʿurbūn), and there is no ق/ث split. The Latin vowel is unstable: oo (English), ou (French-influenced: 'Arboun'), u ('Arbun'). The existing App Store app uses 'Arabon'. German readers may say 'Ar-bohn'. Best single spelling: 'Arboon', with Arboun/Arbun/3arboon as defensive variants.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: 'Ar-boon' suggests 'arbor' and 'boon' (a benefit), which is pleasant and harmless. German: read 'Ar-bohn'; Arbon is a Swiss town on Lake Constance. No meaning. French: the deposit word is 'arrhes', from the same Greek root. 'Arboon' itself means nothing. Turkish: no meaning found (the everyday Turkish for deposit is 'kapora/kaparo', unverified). Cognates: Hebrew ʿeravon (pledge), Greek arrabōn (earnest money), Latin arrha. Modern Greek αρραβώνας also means 'engagement' (unverified). Near-homophone of Arbonne, an MLM brand critics call a pyramid scheme. No vulgar meaning found.
dossiers.sensitivities: The core problem is that the name contradicts the product. The app takes no deposits and no payments. 'Send a deposit before you see it' is the classic online-classifieds scam, and the project's own trust-and-safety advice ('see the item, then pay') is meant to stop exactly that. A brand called 'Deposit' tells users that paying an advance is normal, and every deposit fraud becomes a headline about the brand. Religious-juristic angle: بيع العربون is a known fiqh debate. Fatwa bodies discuss it, the prohibition rests on a hadith against 'بيع العربان', and classical schools differ (the majority are generally reported as disallowing it and the Hanbalis as permitting it). Some devout users may hear a contested transaction. Legal: Syrian Civil Code art. 104 makes the deposit a right-to-withdraw device, which leads to disputes. Not political, sectarian or regional. The figurative 'عربون محبة' softens it only slightly.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Descriptive, verging on deceptively misdescriptive. It names a common payment concept in trade. For a platform that handles no deposits it either describes nothing or misleads. A weak, hard-to-defend mark.

dossiers.meaning_literal: "Our neighbourhood" or "our lane": حارة (quarter, alley) + ـنا (our).
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: An everyday word in both dialect and Standard Arabic. الحارة is the lane where everyone knows everyone, so the word is warm, nostalgic and a bit folksy. Its strongest image is the Damascus old city: حارات الشام and the hit TV series باب الحارة. Homs, Hama, Aleppo, the coast and Hauran also use حارة. In Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa and the Kurdish areas people understand it but more often say حي (inference). A well-known Levantine saying, «حارتنا ضيقة ومنعرف بعض» ("our lane is narrow and we all know each other"), means "you can't fool me". It fits the trust message but has a slightly accusing edge (own knowledge). Elsewhere: in the Gulf (Hijaz, Oman) حارة means an old quarter. In Egypt it means a narrow alley in a working-class district and recalls Mahfouz's novel «أولاد حارتنا». In Lebanon "Haret" is the usual Latin form in place names such as Haret Hreik. Product fit: "our neighbourhood" suggests a hyperlocal social network, but the app searches from 5 to 200 km. The user's Latin spelling is fine. The existing app spells it "Hartna".
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: ح [ħ] sounds the same across Syria (no regional split like ق), but Latin has no letter for it. Writers use H, which merges it with ه, or the Arabizi digit 7 (7aretna). French readers drop the H altogether ("Aretna"). The vowel after r also varies: Levantine ḥārətna (Haretna), Standard Arabic and Gulf ḥāratnā (Haratna), and fast speech Hartna. The name is three syllables, with at least four plausible Latin spellings. The best is Haretna, which matches Syrian speech and the Lebanese "Haret" convention. You would also have to own Hartna, and the existing app already uses that spelling.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: no meaning. It may be read as 'HAIR-et-na'. Nothing embarrassing found. German: H is pronounced, no meaning. French: the H is silent, so it becomes 'Arétna' and the ح is lost; no bad meaning. Turkish: 'hara' means stud farm, which is harmless; 'Haretna' itself has no meaning. Lebanese readers will link 'Haret' to place names such as Haret Hreik in Beirut's southern suburbs (mild). The spelling 'Haaretna' looks like Haaretz, the Israeli newspaper, so avoid the double a. No vulgar sense found. These readings are from knowledge and were not checked against dictionaries this session.
dossiers.sensitivities: Regional: the name reads Damascene and old-city, carried by باب الحارة. Class: حارة شعبية, ابن الحارة and زعران الحارة give it a working-class, folksy tone that some urban middle-class users may not want for a modern app (inference). Literary and religious: across the Arab world «أولاد حارتنا» (Mahfouz, 1959) is the best-known use of the word. The novel was banned in Egypt for decades as blasphemous and is linked to the 1994 knife attack on Mahfouz. This is a mild association, not an insult. Community: "our" lane implies insiders and outsiders. In cities where neighbourhoods map onto communities (e.g. Homs), حارتنا can sound like "our side" (inference). Poverty and privacy: selling household goods to people in your own lane exposes hardship. The app's coarse location and hidden numbers help. Product: it suggests a strictly hyperlocal service, while the app's radius reaches 200 km. No religious or political term in the word itself.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Suggestive but diluted. 'Our neighbourhood' hints at local trade without describing classifieds. But it is an everyday word, already the name of a neighbourhood app with ads (Hartna), and probably common in local business names. Protection would be narrow and contested.

dossiers.meaning_literal: 'Trusted, trustworthy, reliable'. It is the passive participle of وَثِقَ بـ ('to trust in'). It does NOT mean 'verified': that is مُوثَّق (muwaththaq) or «تم التحقق», one و away.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: A Standard Arabic word that every Syrian understands, mainly from set phrases such as «مصدر موثوق» and «محل موثوق». In everyday trading talk Syrians more often call a seller «ثقة» (si'a), «مضمون» or «أمين» (unverified, needs native speakers). It is formal and sounds official, not playful. In speech it is closer to a bank, a ministry or a notary than to a neighbour. Regional readings: (1) Gulf readers, and the many Syrians who live in the Gulf, will think of Saudi Arabia's government 'Mawthooq' licence for social-media advertisers. (2) Egyptian and Lebanese readers take it as plain 'trustworthy'. (3) Turkish speakers have the Ottoman cognate 'mevsuk' ('reliable'); I could not confirm this from TDK. In Syria, the related word توثيق is strongly tied to notarisation and to documenting human-rights violations (inference). No slang sense was found. One risk to test: after the first scam, people may use it sarcastically («موثوق؟!»).
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Two letters that split Syrian pronunciation. ث: city speakers turn it into [s] in learned words (Damascus, Aleppo, Homs: 'mawsūq'), others say [t], and Deir ez-Zor, rural and Bedouin speakers keep [θ]. ق: city speech often has a glottal stop ('mawsū'', typed mawsou2), learned speech keeps [q], and Hauran and Bedouin speakers may say [g]. So one word gives at least four spoken forms. Latin spellings already in use: Mawthooq (the Saudi licence), Mowthooq (Arab News), Mawthuq, Mawthoq (Moltaqa), Mawthok (an iOS shop) and Mawsook (a social app). The Arabic spelling is stable, but dropping the و gives موثق, which leads to notary apps. Best spelling: 'Mawthouq'. The Levantine 'ou' looks different from the Saudi 'Mawthooq' but sounds the same.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: no meaning. Readers split it into 'maw' (an animal's jaws, or dialect for 'mum') and 'thou'. Not embarrassing, but hard to say once and spell. German: W is read as [v] and TH as [t], giving 'Mav-tuk' or 'Mau-tuk'. Colloquial German 'mau' means 'poor, lacklustre' (unverified, minor). French: 'Mo-touk', no meaning found. Turkish: there are no w, q or th sounds, so it is read letter by letter. The Ottoman cognate 'mevsuk' ('reliable') is positive but unverified. No vulgar sense was found in any of these languages.
dossiers.sensitivities: No political, religious, sectarian or regional meaning, and no tie to any city or class. The risks are tone and promise: (1) It sounds official, and its root و-ث-ق is used by Gulf government services (the Saudi licence, Abu Dhabi's Mawthooq platform, the Mwathiq notary app and Wathq) and, in Syria, by notarisation and human-rights documentation (inference). (2) It promises that the app is trusted. But anyone with a +963 number can post, ordinary sellers are not ID-checked, and deals happen by phone. The first scam story ('it's called Trusted') will hurt more than with a neutral name. (3) Brand and badge clash: the planned verified-store badge would naturally be «متجر موثّق», one letter away from the brand. That would imply that the other sellers are not trusted.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Laudatory/descriptive. 'Trusted' names the very quality a marketplace promises. Syria's Law 8/2007 excludes signs that indicate a quality of the product or service, and a Syrian rival (Haraj Syria) already uses the word in its store copy. At best only a logo-plus-word mark would be protected, and the word itself could not be enforced.

dossiers.meaning_literal: 'Barter': swapping goods for goods with no money. It is the Form III verbal noun of قايَضَ, and the fiqh/economics term (بيع المقايضة).
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Every Syrian understands it, but it is MSA and bookish: a word from school economics lessons, the news and fiqh. It is not what people say in the souq or in Facebook ads. There the everyday words are بدّل / تبديل / «للبدل» / «بدّلها» (researcher knowledge, unverified). In the news, «مقايضة» often means a political or state trade-off. Enab Baladi used it for the former government's goods-barter scheme for paying foreign suppliers it could not pay in cash («المقايضة.. وسيلة حكومة النظام العاجزة عن السداد»). It is also used for prisoner swaps and territorial 'deals' (unverified examples). Recent coverage links barter to crisis economies: Lebanon's «لبنان يقايض» Facebook group, and Euronews (July 2026) on barter returning amid inflation. Register: formal, serious, slightly grim. Gulf, Egyptian, Lebanese and Iraqi readers all read it the same way, as 'barter'. Turkish speakers know the cognate 'mukayese', which means 'comparison', not barter.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: It has two problem letters. ق splits by region: a glottal stop in Damascus, Aleppo and Homs (mu'ayaḍa → Arabizi 'M2ayda'); q in Deir ez-Zor, Druze, Alawite and many rural areas ('Mqayada'); g among Bedouin and in Hauran ('Mgayda'). ض is emphatic ḍ in the Levant but merges toward ظ (ð̣) in Mesopotamian eastern Syria, and Arabic users often misspell it as مقايظة (likely, unverified). It has four syllables (mu-qā-ya-ḍa) and at least 10 plausible Latin spellings (q/k/2/g; u/o/ou; final -a/-ah). Store search will split across them. 'Muqayada' is the most scholarly spelling, but no single spelling matches how most Syrians say it.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: no meaning. It looks like an Islamic-finance term; 'muqayyadah' (restricted, as in mudaraba muqayyada) appears in finance glossaries, and Indonesian/Malay readers know it in that sense. German: no meaning. Neither is negative. Kurdish (Kurmanji): no known meaning. No vulgar or embarrassing reading was found in any of these languages.
dossiers.sensitivities: Political: in Syrian news the word means state or political trade-offs, including the former government's goods-barter scheme (Enab Baladi). Class/poverty: barter signals an economy where money has failed (Lebanon crisis groups, Euronews 2026), which is the opposite of a calm, modern marketplace with USD/SYP prices. Product contradiction: the app is cash-for-goods, not barter-only. The name tells users and store reviewers it is a swap app, so people will post swap-only items and expect swap-matching features that do not exist. Religious: it is a neutral fiqh term with no sectarian charge. Regional: none, beyond the ق split.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Descriptive, bordering on generic. It names a type of trading service ('barter'), and Syria's Law No. 8/2007 says signs that indicate the type of service are not distinctive marks. Competitors already use the word freely in titles and descriptions.

key_claims.claim: An iOS shopping app called «سوق المقايضة» already exists for selling products and opening a store, so the same word is already in use in the same category.
Other MENA swap apps use مقايضة as a generic descriptor (Badl: «بدل للمقايضة»), so the word is common property.
Muqayadah is defined in finance glossaries simply as the barter of goods for goods, which shows the term is generic.
Enab Baladi used «المقايضة» for the former Syrian government's goods-barter scheme for paying for imports it could not pay for in cash, which gives the word a political/state association.
Barter is linked in 2026 coverage to inflation and economic crisis, giving it a poverty connotation.
An Iraqi auction app 'Muzayada / مزايدة' (Apr 2026) is one letter away in Latin script.
Deir ez-Zor speech keeps the classical qaf, while urban dialects use a glottal stop, so ق produces regional variants of the name.
Syria's trademark law (Law No. 8/2007) treats signs indicating the type or characteristics of a service as non-distinctive.
Kuwait already has a buy/sell/barter marketplace (Forsa Barter) in the same category.

The word is bookish MSA, it has two problem letters (ق, ض) with no agreed Latin spelling, it is descriptive and unprotectable, «سوق المقايضة» already uses it, and it carries political-trade-off and crisis-economy overtones.

dossiers.meaning_literal: '(It is) lawful/permitted for you': حلال (lawful in Islamic law, the opposite of حرام) + عليك 'on you'.
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: A very common, warm colloquial blessing across the Levant, Egypt and the Gulf. Its senses: 'it's rightfully yours, enjoy it'; a seller's closing words, «مبروك، حلال عليك»; 'keep it, it's yours' when giving something up or forgiving a small debt; and 'well earned / good for you', sometimes sarcastic (researcher knowledge, unverified: searches found no dialect-dictionary source). It is everyday dialect, not formal, and Christians and Druze also use it as an idiom (unverified). The core word is still religious-legal: in MSA and fiqh, حلال is the opposite of حرام. In Gulf/Bedouin Arabic «الحلال» also means livestock or property («حلالك» = your herd/property). Several Saudi and UAE livestock classifieds apps are named حلال, and eastern-Syrian Bedouin speech probably shares this sense (unverified). Turkish has the exact counterpart 'helal olsun' / 'helal sana' ('bravo, you deserve it'), so Turkish speakers would get the positive sense (likely). The fixed phrase also invites the joke opposite «حرام عليك» ('shame on you') whenever a deal goes wrong.
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Two problem letters, ح and ع, which force Arabizi digits ('7alal 3alek', the user's own 'Halal 3alek') or silent loss (Halal Alek). Store search does not reliably map '3' to 'a', according to earlier project findings. عليك varies by region: Damascene/Levantine ʿalēk ('aleik/alek'), Gulf/MSA ʿalayk ('alaik/alayk'), feminine ʿalēki / Gulf ʿalēch. The name is two words with a masculine default. The Latin form also collides with the global word 'Halal'. Best spelling without digits: 'Halal Aleik'. 'ei' signals the Levantine long ē; German readers will say 'alaik', which still matches MSA.
