dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: 'Halal' is read at once as halal-certified food or Islamic finance, so 'Halal Aleik' looks like a halal grocery or a Muslim-only marketplace. German: 'halal' is a known loanword (de.wiktionary) tied to halal meat and to politically charged debates about Islam. Diaspora and non-Muslim German readers would see a religious products app (charged-debate claim unverified). French: halal is politically charged in France, where Muslims use halal apps against a strict secular climate (Arabic Post 2025), so it signals religious identity. Turkish: 'helal' is the exact counterpart, and 'helal olsun' = 'bravo/well deserved', so the reading is positive, but Turks spell it Helal (likely). Arabizi '3' and '7' look odd to all non-Arab readers. No vulgar reading was found.
dossiers.sensitivities: Religious: the core word is an Islamic-legal category. Earlier project research already ruled out حلال as a brand core because it puts off Christians, Druze, Alawites, Ismailis and secular users and reads as a halal-food label. Political/sectarian: in post-2024 Syria, with heightened sectarian tension, a brand built on an Islamic-legal term can be read as signalling religious-conservative alignment (inference). Diaspora: in Germany and France, 'Halal' in Latin script carries political baggage. Regional: the Gulf/Bedouin 'livestock' sense of الحلال. Product: the phrase is also what you say when giving something away free ('keep it'), which blurs the idea of a sale. And scams under this name invite «حرام عليك» jokes, a promise-risk similar to the one earlier research found with Mawthouq.
dossiers.trademark_strength: Suggestive-laudatory idiom built on a generic religious word. The full phrase could be registered as an Arabic+Latin composite, but 'Halal' alone cannot be monopolised (it is generic and descriptive for food and certification). Some MENA offices object to marks with religious significance; whether Syria's Law 8/2007 does so was not verified. Distinctiveness is weak.
dossiers.tagline_en: Sold it? Bought it? Congratulations... it's rightfully yours.

dossiers.verdict_reason: It has the warmest deal-closing meaning of the four, but the brand rests on an Islamic-legal word: it alienates non-Muslim and secular Syrians, reads as halal food or a Muslim-only marketplace to diaspora and international users, and collides with Gulf livestock apps named حلال. It also has ح + ع (Arabizi digits) and two words. Keep «مبروك، حلال عليك» as an in-app message after a sale, not as the brand.

verification.corrections: (1) The 'alienates non-Muslims' claim is overstated for the Arabic idiom, which all communities use. The religious-signalling risk sits mainly in the Latin 'Halal' and in brand-level framing. pan_syrian stays at 2 and low_risk stays at 2 for that reason. (2) meaning_fit is lowered from 4 to 3. The phrase marks the moment a deal closes (and, from the missed haggling sense, the seller giving in on price). It says nothing about posting fast, finding goods nearby, contacting the seller directly or having no middleman. (3) The other scores hold. The verdict is correct: keep «مبروك، حلال عليك» as in-app copy after a sale.

dossiers.best_latin_spelling: Souqak Bibeitak (better: use only 'Souqak' as the Latin wordmark)
dossiers.meaning_literal: 'Your market (is) in your home'. سوقك = 'your market'; ببيتك = colloquial 'in your house' (Standard Arabic: في بيتك).
dossiers.meaning_syrian_usage: Every Syrian and Arab reader understands it at once. It reads as an advertising slogan, not a name. The pattern «السوق ببيتك / سوقك لعندك» is the classic pitch of grocery delivery and e-commerce ('shop without leaving home'), so Syrians will most likely hear 'they deliver'. I could not check this exact phrase. It is dialect (ببيتك) but neutral, with no city flavour. The ending is masculine: a woman is addressed «سوقِك ببيتِك». That looks the same in Arabic script, but the Latin '-ak' is male-only (the same issue as Jaarak). The same letters سَوقك can also be read 'your driving'; this is negligible in context. Gulf, Egyptian and Lebanese readers take it the same way: a home-shopping or delivery slogan. The user's 'Bebeitak' is not a typo, but it adds a vowel that is not spoken; the spoken form is 'b-beitak'. 'Bibeitak' or 'Bbeitak' is closer, and 'Souqak' matches the Levantine 'ou' habit (EzSouq, Souq.com).
dossiers.letters_and_pronunciation: Worst of the four. (1) ق: Damascus, Aleppo, Homs and Hama city speakers say 'Soo'ak' (typed Soo2ak); the coast, Druze, rural areas and Deir ez-Zor keep 'Sooqak'; Hauran and Bedouin speakers say 'Soogak'. (2) بيت: city speakers say [bēt] (beit/bet), while rural and Bedouin speakers say [bayt] (bait/bayt). The doubled b ('bbēt') has no obvious Latin form (Bebeitak, Bbeitak, Bibeitak, Bi beitak). (3) It is two words and four or five syllables. Latin variants multiply: about 6 forms for سوقك × 6 for ببيتك. It needs the Arabizi '2' for the city pronunciation. If kept, use 'Souqak' alone as the Latin wordmark, with the full Arabic phrase.

dossiers.foreign_language_issues: English: 'Souk' is known (from tourism) as 'market', which is fine. But 'Sooqak Bebeitak' is unpronounceable on first sight, and 'Bebe-' reads like 'baby'. French: colloquial 'c'est le souk' means 'it's a mess, chaos', the same problem the earlier notes found with 'bazar' (author's knowledge, unverified). 'Bébé' means 'baby'. German: no meaning. 'Souk' is a known tourist word; 'Bebeitak' has none. Turkish: 'Soukak' or 'Sukak' sounds like 'sokak' ('street, alley'). Harmless, even friendly. Dutch and Afrikaans: the variant 'Soukak' ends in 'kak' (vulgar for excrement). Minor, and avoided by spelling it 'Souqak'. No serious vulgar sense was found.
dossiers.sensitivities: No political, religious, sectarian or regional meaning. It is not tied to one city or class. Main problem, a contradiction with the product: 'the market comes to your home' implies delivery or home shopping. This app does not deliver; buyers meet sellers nearby and arrange the handover by phone. Users who expect delivery will be disappointed or confused, and it invites comparison with delivery apps (BeeOrder, YallaGo). The masculine address leaves out women in the Latin form. The سوق root also recalls the informal «سوق الحرامية» ('thieves' market') second-hand trade only by association (negligible).
dossiers.trademark_strength: Descriptive, plus a laudatory slogan. سوق names the service itself (a marketplace), and 'in your home' describes convenience. Law 8/2007's exclusion of descriptive signs makes the words unregistrable on their own. A logo mark would give only narrow protection, and the سوق root is shared by at least 14 Syria-facing apps.

dossiers.verdict_reason: It is a slogan, not a name. It sits on the most crowded root in Syrian classifieds (سوق), it is descriptive (very weak trademark), and it is two words with ق and many Latin spellings. Worse, it promises home delivery, which the app does not offer. If the user likes the idea, it could at most become a reframed campaign line under another brand («تصفّح من بيتك، واشتري من جارك»).
